title: Bromcom - 355,051 breached accounts
summary: In September 2026, UK education software provider Bromcom suffered a data breach involving a legacy single sign-on (SSO) registration system. The incident exposed 355k unique email addresses belonging to staff and pupils at UK schools, alongside SSO registration reference numbers. Bromcom confirmed that no passwords or authentication tokens were exposed, and that the incident did not enable access to Microsoft or Google accounts or its school management system.

title: Too Lost - 724,323 breached accounts
summary: In November 2026, an unauthorised party claimed to have obtained data from the music distributor for independent artists, Too Lost. The data contained 724k unique email addresses belonging to artists, their collaborators and fans. Some records also contained bcrypt password hashes, while a small subset included partial credit card data (last 4 digits and card type), identity verification information (in some cases, passport, driver's licence or national ID numbers), and payouts made to artists. Too Lost advised that its investigation remains ongoing, external forensic specialists have been engaged, and measures have been taken to secure affected systems and credentials. The company is also working with advisors to coordinate communications and support for affected individuals.

The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham?

Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.”

I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’”

Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human.

Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband.

Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong.

So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’”

I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity.

Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday. But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes.

His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe.

AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them.

Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the sea and surfing here, and a gentle tapping into surfing’s spiritual side; a handful of gorgeous scenes in a palette of mushroom brown and grey tell snippets of its origins in Polynesia. At heart, In Waves is an idealistic, emotional film, handling its subject delicately, avoiding too much of the rawness of grief. I can imagine older kids and teenagers falling deeply in love with it.

At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado. In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was.

Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning over the tricksy rhythmic figures of the faster movements and radiating warmth in the third, which sounded like Cole Porter reflected in a slightly warped mirror. Mullov-Abbado’s violin writing is as gratifying as you’d hope for from the son of Viktoria Mullova, and his jazz-classical fusion hits an unusually effective sweet spot.

She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation.

Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own.

Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”.

Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour.

It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something.
